course.learn: A false positive occurs when a security tool reports a problem or malicious event that is not actually present.
course.why: Too many false positives create analyst fatigue and waste investigation time.
course.example: A vulnerability scanner flags a package as vulnerable even though the vendor backported the security fix without changing the version string.

course.learn: A false negative occurs when a real security problem exists but the tool fails to detect or report it.
course.why: False negatives are dangerous because defenders may believe the environment is safe while risk remains active.
course.example: Malware runs on an endpoint but the detection tool classifies the behavior as normal and generates no alert.
course.exam: False negative = missed threat; usually more dangerous than a false positive.

course.learn: Vulnerability classification and prioritization combine technical severity with exposure, exploitability, asset importance, business impact, compliance, available controls, and current threat activity.
course.why: Fixing vulnerabilities in score order alone can waste resources or leave the most dangerous business risk exposed.
course.example: An actively exploited medium-severity flaw on an Internet-facing domain controller is prioritized over a higher-scoring issue on an offline test machine.

defs: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a framework used to score vulnerability severity.

course.learn: CVSS is a standardized framework for rating the technical severity of vulnerabilities using factors such as attack requirements and impact.
course.why: A severity score helps compare findings, but organizations still need business and environmental context to prioritize work.
course.example: A CVSS 9.8 flaw on an isolated lab system may be lower priority than a 7.5 flaw on a critical Internet-facing payment server.
course.exam: CVSS = severity score. Do not use score alone for risk priority.

defs: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the standardized identifier assigned to a publicly known vulnerability.

course.learn: CVE provides standardized identifiers for publicly known vulnerabilities so vendors, scanners, researchers, and defenders can refer to the same issue consistently.
course.why: A shared identifier makes it easier to correlate advisories, patches, and scanner findings.
course.example: A scanner reports CVE-20XX-12345 and the administrator uses that identifier to find the vendor advisory and patch.
